title: Polynomial-time refutation of random 3-SAT at constant density
formal:
Do there exist an integer \(C\geq6\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) such that \(A\) never outputs \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) on any satisfiable \(3\)-CNF formula, and
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{F\sim R_3(n,Cn),\,\rho}
 [A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNSAT}]=1?
\]
The distribution \(R_3\), exact soundness, and worst-case time bound are defined below. The constant \(C\), machine and its time polynomial must be fixed before \(n\); the probability includes the algorithm’s independent random bits \(\rho\).
definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. General inputs are explicitly listed \(3\)-CNF formulas, with at most three literals in each clause; repeated clauses, repeated literals and empty clauses are allowed. The empty clause is false. The number \(n\) of named variables and the list length are encoded in binary, followed by binary indices and sign bits with delimiters. Valid indices lie in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\); unused variables are allowed. Let \(L\) be the complete encoded length. Malformed encodings receive \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\) in polynomial time.

For \(n\geq3\), the random distribution \(R_3(n,m)\) is an ordered list of \(m\) independent clauses sampled with replacement. For each clause choose a uniformly random three-element subset of \([n]\), and independently negate each selected variable with probability \(1/2\). Write its three variables in index order. Thus each random clause has three distinct variables, duplicate clauses may occur, and signs in all clauses are independent. This fixed-size distribution is not a planted distribution or a distribution conditioned on unsatisfiability.

The algorithm always outputs either \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) or \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). Exact soundness means that for every satisfiable input formula \(F\) and every sequence \(\rho\) of its random bits, \(A(F;\rho)=\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\). On an unsatisfiable formula it may also return \(\mathrm{UNKNOWN}\); the required frequency of success applies only to the stated random distribution. Even on exceptional input formulas or random choices there is no allowed false assertion of unsatisfiability.

Use a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine with independent fair bits and no advice or external oracle. There must be integers \(K,d\geq1\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations on every input and every random-bit sequence, including adversarial formulas. Reading random bits and producing the answer are charged, so only polynomially many bits may be used. This is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time bound on random formulas. Deterministic machines are included.

The probability limit requires that for every real \(\eta>0\) there is an integer \(n_0\) such that for every integer \(n\geq\max\{3,n_0\}\), the probability of \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) is at least \(1-\eta\). The rate of convergence need not be supplied as an algorithm. The density \(C\) is an absolute constant, not a function tending to infinity with \(n\). Choosing integer \(C\geq6\) loses no successful smaller constant-density regime: on a denser input the algorithm can run a lower-density refuter on the appropriate clause prefix, whose distribution is exactly the lower-density model. Unsatisfiability of a prefix implies unsatisfiability of the full formula, preserving soundness.

No named proof system or explicit derivation format is imposed. The output \(\mathrm{UNSAT}\) must be justified by the proven soundness of the algorithm; the machine need not print a resolution or sum-of-squares proof. Existence of short unsatisfiability certificates without an efficient way of finding them does not meet this definition.

context_blocks.text: Typical unsatisfiability has a short counting proof. For any fixed assignment, a random clause is satisfied with probability \(7/8\), so the expected number of satisfying assignments in \(R_3(n,Cn)\) is \(2^n(7/8)^{Cn}\). For \(C\geq6\), this tends to zero exponentially. Markov’s inequality therefore shows that the formula is unsatisfiable with probability tending to one. Always printing UNSAT would exploit that statistical fact but would violate soundness on satisfiable inputs.

The task asks for a certificate on a particular input while exploiting its typical structure. Search and proof existence are separate: a family of short refutations does not by itself give a polynomial-time algorithm that finds one. The 2015 source explicitly separates these possibilities in its comparison of efficient refutation algorithms and nondeterministically available certificates.

Spectral and semidefinite methods give efficient refutation at much higher clause counts, around \(n^{3/2}\) for random \(3\)-SAT in the source’s historical account. The relevant density is the number of clauses divided by \(n\), so this regime grows like \(\sqrt n\), in contrast to the constant required here. A bound for other predicates, such as not-all-equal clauses, cannot be substituted for ordinary disjunction clauses.

Gap refutation proves that every assignment violates a positive fraction of clauses. It must therefore remain silent even on suitable nearly satisfiable formulas. Barak’s cited formulation of Feige’s hypothesis uses this stronger soundness requirement. The present target retains the previously approved requirement of soundness only on satisfiable formulas, so consequences of a gap hypothesis must be checked separately.

The 2026 work extends the density, relaxation degree and refutation-strength tradeoff to more general random CSP distributions without uniformly random literals. Its sum-of-squares lower bounds restrict a particular family of algebraic relaxations; its generalization of the upper bounds does not supply the unrestricted constant-density algorithm asked for here. The paper treats binomial random-instance models in its displayed theorems, another reason to avoid identifying them verbatim with this fixed-size target.

The August 2026 ECCC report states stronger lower bounds for resolution extended to bounded-width disjunctions of conjunctions. Such a result blocks algorithms restricted to those refutations, but it does not rule out a different sound polynomial-time computation. The claim is recorded at the abstract level rather than as an independent full-proof audit.

If \(\mathsf P=\mathsf{NP}\), a deterministic polynomial-time SAT decision algorithm can refute every unsatisfiable input, and the elementary counting argument gives the required average-case success. Consequently an unconditional negative answer here would imply \(\mathsf P\ne\mathsf{NP}\). A positive answer would be a distribution-specific algorithm and would not itself decide worst-case SAT.

why: This problem isolates the gap between knowing that a typical sparse formula is unsatisfiable and efficiently proving unsatisfiability without ever making a false claim. A resolution would identify a major limit of average-case certification or produce an algorithm beyond the methods underlying existing refutation barriers.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply one constant \(C\), one uniform algorithm, its worst-case polynomial time bound, exact soundness for every satisfiable input and every random-bit sequence, and the success limit for \(R_3(n,Cn)\).

A negative answer must rule out every such constant and every such algorithm. Equivalently, for every proposed sound polynomial-time \(A\) and every integer \(C\geq6\), there must be some \(\eta>0\) such that failure probability is at least \(\eta\) for arbitrarily large \(n\). Showing failure for a single algorithm, proof system or finite set of inputs is insufficient. A conditional theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional target. Algorithms requiring a growing clause density, allowing erroneous refutations on rare satisfiable inputs, or merely distinguishing a planted distribution do not satisfy the criterion.

importance.reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.

progress.text: Barak records a Feige-hypothesis formulation with soundness on nearly satisfiable instances, which is stronger than the exact-satisfiability condition retained here.
Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer give general random-CSP refutation algorithms and separate exact-sound refutation, gap refutation, planted detection and existence of short certificates.
Chan, d’Orsi and Xu extend SoS and spectral tradeoffs to predicates without uniformly random literals; the displayed results concern these algorithmic families and their density requirements.
An ECCC report states improved constant-density lower bounds within k-DNF resolution; this is proof-system evidence, not a lower bound against every sound refuter.

status_note: The 2015 primary source poses efficient random-3-SAT refutation as a major challenge and explicitly defines exact soundness. The 30 April 2026 paper and the August 2026 ECCC abstract concern SoS/spectral tradeoffs and k-DNF resolution, respectively; neither states a solution for unrestricted sound polynomial-time refutation at constant density. Checked 16 September 2026. This is a bounded source review, not a proof of universal current openness or an independent verification of every cited lower bound.

source_formulation.text: Can a sound polynomial-time algorithm refute almost all random 3-SAT instances already at some constant clause density?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the exact-sound refutation problem discussed in §1, with the previously approved fixed-size distribution and existential constant-density target made explicit.

sentences: A random 3-SAT formula at sufficiently large constant clause density is almost surely unsatisfiable.
The question asks for one polynomial-time randomized refuter that recognizes almost all such formulas while never rejecting a satisfiable formula.
The density, algorithm and time bound must be fixed independently of the number of variables.
Gap refutation, planted detection and lower bounds for particular proof systems do not settle this exact-sound unrestricted target.
An accepted answer proves existence or impossibility with the full quantifiers in Lean.
